overview:
While Moses is on the mountain, the people press Aaron to make them gods to go before them. He melts their gold earrings into a calf, builds an altar, and proclaims a feast to the LORD. God tells Moses to go down and threatens to consume the people and start over with him; Moses pleads, and God relents. Coming down, Moses sees the dancing, smashes the tables, grinds the calf to powder, and makes Israel drink it. The Levites rally to him and about three thousand fall. Moses goes back up to seek atonement, asking to be blotted out of God’s book if the people are not forgiven.

Moses talks God out of his anger on the mountain, then loses his own at the foot of it. The same verb, “wax hot,” is used of God’s wrath (vv. 10–11) and of Moses’ anger when he sees the calf (v. 19).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Tradition credits Moses; many scholars see older sources combined in Exodus.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses’ lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); scholarly proposals reach the 6th–5th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: At the end of Moses’ forty days on Sinai (24:18), in Israel’s first year out of Egypt. The exodus is dated about 1446 BC from 1 Kings 6:1, or to the 13th century BC on a common scholarly view.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The camp at the foot of Sinai (Horeb) and the mountain above it.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Deuteronomy 9:7–21, Moses’ own retelling. The Joseph Smith Translation revises vv. 12 and 14.

hermeneutics:
Bulls stood for divine strength across Canaan. Ugaritic texts call the high god “Bull El,” and in 1990 excavators at Ashkelon found a small silver-plated bronze calf from about 1600 BC inside a pottery shrine. Storm gods were often shown standing on a bull’s back. Many scholars think Aaron’s calf was meant as a pedestal or emblem of the LORD, since he proclaims “a feast to the LORD” (v. 5). Either way, the text treats it as a plain breach of the commands against images and gods of gold (20:4, 23).

In the Ugaritic Baal Cycle the goddess Anat destroys Mot, the god of death, in a fixed series: she splits him with a blade, winnows him, burns him with fire, grinds him with millstones, and scatters him in the field. Moses does nearly the same to the calf. He burns it, grinds it to powder, and scatters it on water (v. 20). Scholars (Loewenstamm) read the match as a stock way of describing the total destruction of a god. Here the god is a lump of metal, and the people drink what is left of it.

Centuries later Jeroboam set up two golden calves at Bethel and Dan for the northern kingdom and introduced them with Aaron’s words, “behold thy gods, O Israel” (1 Kings 12:28). Both calves were offered as images of the God who brought Israel out of Egypt, and that is exactly what the text condemns. A reader who knew the history of the kings would hear the northern kingdom’s sin already present at Sinai.

breakdown.label: The people demand gods; Aaron makes the calf; a feast
On the mountain: God’s wrath and his offer to Moses
Moses pleads: remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel; the LORD relents
Moses descends, breaks the tables, destroys the calf
Aaron’s excuse: “there came out this calf”
“Who is on the LORD’s side?”: the Levites; three thousand fall
Moses returns to make atonement: “blot me … out of thy book”

notes: **Who brought them up?** “Brought … out of the land of Egypt” comes 6 times (vv. 1, 4, 7, 8, 11, 23), and the credit keeps moving: the people give it to Moses, then to the calf; God, speaking to Moses, calls them “thy people, which thou broughtest”; Moses answers that they are God’s people, whom God brought forth.
**A great sin:** the phrase comes 3 times in Hebrew (vv. 21, 30, 31): Moses says it to Aaron, then to the people, then to God.
Each mountain scene ends with only a partial answer. God relents from destroying the people (v. 14), then puts off punishment to “the day when I visit” (v. 34).

Chapters 32–34 break into the tabernacle story: the instructions end at 31:18 and the building starts at 35:1. The calf breaks the covenant sealed in ch. 24, and these chapters ask whether God’s presence can still go with Israel. The answer comes in 34:10: “Behold, I make a covenant.”

**Echoes later:** Psalm 106:19–20 remembers that Israel “changed their glory” for the likeness of an ox, and Deuteronomy 9–10 has Moses recall the calf and the second tables before Israel enters the land.

traditions.text: In the KJV Moses asks God to repent, and the LORD “repented” (vv. 12, 14). The Joseph Smith Translation changes both verses: Moses says “Thy people will repent of this evil,” and the Lord answers that if they repent he will spare them, while Moses is to execute judgment on all who will not repent that day. The repentance becomes the people’s, and it prepares for the Levites’ work in vv. 26–28.

Explains what was lost at Sinai. Moses sought to sanctify his people so they could behold the face of God, but they hardened their hearts and could not endure his presence. The Lord swore in his wrath that they would not enter his rest, took Moses and the holy priesthood out of their midst, and left the lesser priesthood and “the law of carnal commandments” with the house of Aaron.

Abinadi explains why Israel received a very strict law: they were “a stiffnecked people,” the words God uses in v. 9, quick to do iniquity and slow to remember him. So they were given a law of performances and ordinances to keep them in remembrance of God, and all of it, he adds, pointed to things to come.

Reads the word for “delayed” in v. 1 as two words, “six has come.” Moses had promised to return after forty days at the sixth hour; Satan darkened the world with a storm, told the people Moses was dead, and showed them an image of his bier in the clouds. Rashi adds that the people counted the day of his ascent and so expected him a day early.

Hur, it says, rebuked the people and was killed, which is why Aaron built the altar in fear. The women refused to give up their earrings, so the men gave their own. When Moses saw the dancing, the writing flew off the tables and they grew too heavy to hold, so he let them fall; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on v. 19 also has the holy writing fly away.
traditions.cite: Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 45; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Exodus 32:19

traditions.text: Rabbi Abbahu notes that God says “let me alone” (v. 10) before Moses has said a word. He takes it to mean that Moses had seized hold of God like a man grabbing his friend by the garment and would not let go until the people were forgiven. Were the verse not written, he says, no one would dare to say it.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says Israel made the calf only to give an opening to penitents. A people who had just heard God at Sinai should not have been capable of it, so the story shows that even a whole community’s worst sin can be repented of, as David’s showed for one man. The JST’s “if they will repent” (above) puts the same hope into the text.

In the synagogue the first account of the calf is read aloud and translated, but the second is read without translation. The Mishnah lists it with other passages handled the same way, such as Reuben’s sin with Bilhah, and later commentators identify the second account as Aaron’s report in vv. 21–24.

Philo says the people became “eager imitators of the Egyptian inventions” and made a golden calf after the animal held most sacred in that land. He does not name it, though Egypt’s best-known sacred bull was the Apis of Memphis. The Levites who answered Moses’ call proved their zeal, Philo says, and received the temple service as their reward, as Numbers 3:12 later sets them apart.

Josephus describes the people’s fear while Moses was gone forty days, some saying wild beasts had killed him and others that he had gone to God. Then Moses returns to general joy, with the tables in hand. The golden calf is missing; Josephus leaves it out entirely and never says why.

Stephen retells v. 1 almost word for word and says the fathers turned back to Egypt in their hearts and rejoiced in the works of their own hands. Paul quotes v. 6, the people sat down to eat and drink and “rose up to play,” as a warning to the Corinthians against idolatry.

Barnabas quotes v. 7 and says that when Moses cast the tables from his hands, “their covenant was broken.” In his reading Israel lost the covenant at the moment it was given, so that the covenant of Jesus could be sealed on Christian hearts. D&C 84 also says something was taken away at Sinai, though it speaks of the higher priesthood and leaves a lesser law in force.

Irenaeus holds that God first asked of Israel only the Ten Commandments. When they made the calf and turned back to Egypt in their minds, he says, they were placed under a further law suited to their wish, a yoke of bondage, and he cites Ezekiel 20:24 and Stephen’s speech. His picture of a law added because of the calf is close to D&C 84 and Mosiah 13 (above).
